title: The Closed Hand
logline: A family workshop takes on an apprentice from outside the family. The craft passes hand to hand in daily lessons, but some steps are only ever done when the apprentice has gone home.
human_question: What is the difference between a skill you protect and a skill you keep to yourself?

premise.story: The daily rhythm of teaching a hereditary craft to an apprentice who is not family: open demonstrations, quiet conversations between family members about how much to show, and the apprentice's own progress and frustrations over weeks or months.
premise.place: A small family metalworking or casting workshop where a technique has passed down through generations.
premise.experience: The viewer learns the craft alongside the apprentice, at exactly the pace they are allowed to learn it, and feels the pull between a family protecting its livelihood and a student wanting to be trusted with all of it.

concept_links.why: Both sources count knowledge or skill (dhamma) among the five things this state of mind clings to and will not let go: as much a target of stinginess as a house, a following, a reputation or a gain [C022-P:L133–L135; C022-M:L43–L45]. A hereditary craft, taught to an outsider, is a direct, filmable form of exactly that pull.

This state is unusual: it grows out of attachment to one's own things, yet it shows itself as displeasure at those things being shared, so the sources group it with aversion rather than with wanting [C026-M:L19]. What looks like simple caution or love for the craft may, in a given moment, be either wanting to keep, or displeasure at sharing; the film need not decide which, only observe closely.

what_camera_could_observe: Open teaching: demonstrations, corrections, the apprentice's hands learning
Family conversations, in the family's own words, about what and how much to teach
Moments the apprentice is asked to step away, and what happens after they do
The apprentice's own account of what they notice being withheld, if anything
Work leaving the workshop, finished by whichever hands actually finished it
what_must_be_real: The workshop, the family and the apprentice's real teaching relationship must be genuine and already in progress. Trade methods the family wishes to keep private must stay private; the film observes the relationship, not the secret itself.

possible_arc.opening: A finished piece, and the many unseen hands and steps behind it.
possible_arc.turn: A specific moment of teaching, or of being asked to step aside, makes the pull visible.
possible_arc.ending_open: Whatever the family and the apprentice actually decide about how far the teaching goes ends the film.

requirements: A hereditary craft workshop currently training an apprentice from outside the family
Consent from the family to show what they are comfortable showing, and no more
An apprentice willing to speak about their own experience of the teaching

suggestions.name: A family brass or metalwork workshop
suggestions.why: A region with a long-standing tradition of hereditary metal-craft workshops, some still family-run and training-based.
suggestions.verify: A specific workshop currently training an outside apprentice must be found and confirmed; this is a region-level suggestion only.

risks: Framing a family's protection of its livelihood as a moral failing
Exposing trade methods the family wishes to keep private
The apprentice feeling exposed by speaking honestly about what is withheld from them
drop_if: No workshop is currently training a non-family apprentice
The family is unwilling to have the teaching relationship itself observed

connections.note: Both examine what people will or won't share: a skill in one, a catch in the other.
Two workshops of willingness: one about giving knowledge freely or not, one about giving effort freely or not.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
